newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Le Pen embraces Bosnian Serb ultra-nationalists.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen embraces Bosnian Serb ultra-nationalists.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen hailed ultra-nationalist leaders of Bosnia's Serb republic on Thursday as misunderstood heroes.
Le Pen toured the Serb government seat of Pale, a mountain village outside Sarajevo, as part of a three-day visit at the invitation of the hardline nationalist Serbian Radical Party.
"I wish to convey to your people greetings from French patriots," Le Pen told the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, as reporters looked on.
"There are many who do not know any more what it is to be attached to one's land and to one's country.

"But we who have a country share the same feeling and understand very well that all patriots of the world still have in common identical values and we make up one community of civilised men and women."

Krajisnik welcomed Le Pen's comments, saying: "Your words are like a remedy for the soul and we understand them completely." He said Western countries had "tried to demonise" the Serbs and failed to understand the 3-1/2 year Bosnian war.
Le Pen was treated as an honoured guest by the same Serb leaders whose army fired on French U.N. peacekeeping soldiers during the war.
The 68-year-old politician and the Serb nationalists share a hostility towards co-existence with those of the Islamic faith.
Le Pen has led his National Front party to prominence by playing to anti-immigrant sentiment in France, winning votes with tirades against Arab immigrants from North Africa.
He visited the Serbian capital Belgrade on Tuesday accompanied by the leader of the Radical party, Vojislav Seselj.
Le Pen was scheduled to have lunch later with Serb political leaders at presidential offices in Pale.
The presidential compound, located in the grounds of a factory, is known as the headquarters of wartime Bosnian Serb president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
There was no official confirmation whether Karadzic, who still wields power behind the scenes, dined with Le Pen.
Le Pen's visit sparked controversy at home in the ranks of his own party where pro-Croatian sympathisers are particularly powerful.

The daily newspaper Present, voice of ultra-traditionalist Catholics in the FN, wrote last week that "simpletons in our own political family who try to pass off the killer Seselj as a so-called nationalist opponent to the 'Serbolshevik' Milosevic demonstrate their complete ignorance of the situation."
FN Euro-parliamentarian Bernard Antony issued a statement on Thursday "aimed at cutting short attempts to de-stabilise the National Front about our leader's visit to Serbia".
Antony said Le Pen told him before leaving that his visit "would in no case be aimed at approving the bellicose demands of this or that Serb faction, particularly concerning Croatia".
Le Pen has wrong-footed his own supporters on foreign policy twice before, each time provoking angry debate which has since apparently subsided in the Front National.
The first case was in the 1990 Gulf War when Le Pen publicly backed Iraqi President Saddam Hussein even though the French army was pitted against his forces on the battlefield.

More recently he made a highly publicised visit to Moscow to befriend Russian rightist Vladimir Zhirinovsky who had until then been violently denounced by FN-linked publications as a former Communist agent seeking to bring back Communism.
